source.title: Curvature-based Comparison of Two Neural Networks
source.authors: Tao Yu; Huan Long; J. Hopcroft

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares representations from independently trained networks using manifold geometry, Euclidean distances, curvature distributions, and linear-map RMSE rather than the original studies' methods.
record.gate_note: The paper compares two AlexNet implementations with the same architecture, trained independently with different initial parameters and similar accuracy. It reports several geometric comparisons, but does not vary model scale, architecture, objective, or modality. Its curvature and distance results concern Goldfish inputs; Table III reports percentages across the total images without stating their number in the text. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Compares two same-architecture AlexNets trained from different initializations, using local distance matrices, a fitted linear map and curvature distributions. These are different methods aimed at the V3/V4 question of whether independently trained networks learn the same representations.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the two AlexNets share local manifold properties: similar lengths, distance matrices, small full-dimensional RMSE and equal dimensions. Tangent-space projections differ, and a linear map cannot explain the difference. Curvature distributions match for many images, which the authors read as extracting the same features, but differ for others, where they say the networks extract different features despite the same classification. They propose curvature as a comparison criterion beyond Euclidean methods.
record.recipe_differences: Compares activation-manifold geometry, Euclidean distances, curvature distributions, and least-squares transformation errors; does not use a scale sweep or the original studies' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported similarity varies by layer and by curvature measure (Riemann versus sectional curvature); the authors also report different curvature matches for different images.
record.problems: Only two models are compared, with the same architecture and close accuracy; no model scale or capability variation is tested. Many quantitative comparisons focus on Goldfish data. The paper notes that some curvature distributions do not match, and reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Table II's activation-vector norms, cross-model distances for corresponding activations, and ranks are omitted because they do not directly report similarity of induced pairwise distances or a separate mapping outcome beyond the RMSE rows. Figure-only curvature curves are not separately catalogued; the text and Table III provide the quantitative curvature results.

untested.parts: No scale, capability, architecture, objective or data variation; only two same-architecture AlexNets with close accuracy.
No unit-level or explicit feature matching and no subspace-overlap measure; convolutional layers excluded; only one pair of seeds.
No held-out evaluation of the map, no stitching, no relative representations, no mapping without paired data.
No interpretable neurons, SAE features or circuits.
No systematic variation of metric settings and no out-of-distribution inputs; mostly one class (Goldfish).
No plateau over scale; does not test whether shared data or objectives explain the alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The two models are bvlc_alexnet and bvlc_reference_caffenet. The paper calls them identical in structure; CaffeNet is commonly described as swapping pooling and normalization order, so this may not be a pure seed comparison. Not verified from the text. All quantitative results are for Goldfish only. The image count behind Table III is not stated (Table I uses 150 patches). Sorting curvature values discards axis correspondence, so the curvature match tests distributional rather than feature identity. Pre-dates both original sources' framings but cites Convergent Learning [20].

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep; the compared models have the same architecture and similar accuracy.
No vision-language or paired image-caption comparison.
Does not compare individual units, explicit features, or shared subspaces; compares geometric properties of representations from two initializations of the same architecture.
Tests a scaling-and-rotation linear transformation with translation on Goldfish data; does not test stitching, relative representations, or mapping without paired data.
Does not identify or compare interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Compares Euclidean and curvature-based measures, and reports differing results across images; does not systematically vary metric settings or test out-of-distribution inputs.

Reports incomplete agreement for some inputs under shared architecture and training context, but does not test a plateau over scale or compare shared-data/objective explanations against a common-reality explanation.

rows.subject: AlexNet1 to AlexNet2
rows.operation_detail: Fit a scaling-and-rotation matrix and translation to normalized original activation data by least squares.
rows.baseline: Mean cross-model distance of corresponding normalized activations: 36
rows.locator: Section III-A, Table II and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper says the RMSE is small relative to the corresponding-activation distance, but also reports a small decrease in rank after transformation.
rows.check: RMSE 0.76 against a corresponding-activation distance of 36 is about 2%, so state should be observed, not partial. However, the fit is in-sample in 4096 dimensions, with patch rank 738 and no held-out test. Rank drops 738→618, so the low error is weak evidence.

source_check.locator_found: Section III-A, Table II: C6 normalized corresponding distance 36; original-data RMSE 0.76.
